ls-sell-online: Key Highlights Selling land is a legal transfer with a fixed sequence — the portal only finds the buyer. Before listing: title, mutation, classification, encumbrance status and tax records all verified in YOUR name. The transfer happens through a registered sale deed — never through the listing or the agreement. Cross ₹50 lakh (resident sale) and the buyer deducts 1% TDS; rural agricultural land is outside TDS entirely. Mutation after registration is the forgotten step — and the one that moves the tax bills to the new owner. What selling land legally involves Under the Transfer of Property Act, a sale hands over all rights in the property for a price. The seller’s classic confusion mirrors the buyer’s: the sale agreement is the blueprint — price, schedule, possession date, binding — while only the registered deed moves ownership. Wherever the buyer comes from — portal or neighbour’s cousin — the sequence is identical: verify your own papers, agree terms, sign the agreement, duty, registration, mutation. The paperwork a seller needs ready Title deed; a fresh EC showing no hidden mortgage or dispute; current tax receipts; any NOCs the local authority requires; and for inherited land, the succession papers — probate where applicable, legal-heir documentation — that prove your RIGHT to sell. Before a single listing goes up: title clear, mutation showing YOUR name (buyers walk away from unmutated sellers), encumbrances verified, taxes cleared. Example: A seller lists inherited land, finds a buyer in a week — then spends four months assembling heirship papers while the buyer’s lawyer waits. The land was always sellable; the FILE was not. Preparation is what “luck” looks like from outside. How the sale process works List → lock the buyer → sign the agreement → TDS if applicable → registered deed at the SRO with full duty → mutation. Registration does not end the seller’s job: hand over possession, ORIGINAL documents, keys if any, and clear pending utility bills. Mutation — usually the buyer’s application — flips the state’s records and the tax liability; a decent seller helps it happen. Red flags that stall sales Stale mutation entries; unclear ownership history; pending encumbrances; unpaid taxes; missing NOCs; wrong land classification; an unlinked PAN; and for NRI sellers, a PoA without proper attestation — which stalls registration exactly as hard as a title defect. Sale agreement vs sale deed — seller’s view Aspect Sale agreement Sale deed Purpose Records the agreed terms Legally transfers ownership Nature Private contract Registered with the Sub-Registrar Effect Binds terms; moves nothing Completes the transfer Use Locks price and possession during negotiation The final closing document Cost Minimal stamping Full duty + registration fees Whatever is written into an agreement, the land stays legally yours until the deed registers — which is also why you never hand over possession or originals early: sequence is the seller’s only real protection. Choosing where to list Land-specific platforms suit agricultural and open plots — buyers there search by survey number and approval status, not floor plans; the big general portals bring broader traffic for land near city edges. Whatever the platform: it finds buyers; it transfers nothing; and its “verification” badge never substitutes for your own file. Tax obligations on the sale TDS (Section 194-IA) : resident sales at ₹50 lakh or more — the buyer deducts 1% on the higher of price and stamp-duty value, filing Form 26QB. Rural agricultural land is not a capital asset, so no TDS. NRI sellers fall under Section 195 at higher rates — a lower/nil-deduction certificate obtained IN ADVANCE is the planning move. Capital gains are computed on the higher of price and guideline value — know both numbers before agreeing either. Pre-listing checklist ☐ Title deed + history verified. ☐ Fresh EC. ☐ Mutation shows your name. ☐ Tax receipts current. ☐ NOCs collected. ☐ PAN linked with Aadhaar. ☐ Succession papers ready for inherited land. ☐ Classification verified before listing. Quick answers (FAQ) Can an NRI sell remotely? Yes — through a properly attested, registered PoA, with Section 195 TDS handled. How long does the whole process take? With a ready file: weeks. With a broken file: months, and sometimes the buyer. Is registration mandatory? Always — no registered deed, no transfer, whatever was signed or paid. Bottom line Land sells fastest when the paperwork is ready before the buyer is. Title, mutation and a linked PAN fixed early cost nothing; discovered mid-negotiation they cost the tempo, the price, and sometimes the deal. For you: Flip this lesson into product: hand every plot buyer of yours a closing kit — deed copy, EC, mutation guidance. The developer whose buyers’ paperwork sails is the developer whose next venture pre-sells. Original Deccan Ledger lesson; full source article on 1acre.in (links above). ls-buy-agri: Key Highlights Eligibility is state law, not national: some states restrict to farmers, others let anyone buy. Ceiling laws cap the total holding — and the cap moves by state and land type. Verification means pulling deed, EC and revenue records YOURSELF — most disputes start in skipped paperwork. The negotiated price is the start of spending: duty, registration, legal and survey fees stack on top. NRIs cannot buy farmland outright — inheritance is their route in. Who can legally buy The land’s state decides, through its land-reform laws. Restricted states demand an agricultural background or eligibility test (with exemption and family routes for some non-farmers); open states — Telangana included — let anyone buy. On top sits the ceiling: a cap on total holdings that varies by state and land type, and crossing it can void the excess. Confirm both BEFORE attachment to a plot sets in. What verification covers, and why The step that decides whether the purchase becomes an asset or a decade of correspondence. The core: title deed — name matches the seller; EC for 15–30 years — loans and claims; latest revenue records — ownership and classification cross-checked (pattadar passbook in Telangana); mutation — actually updated, because an unmutated transfer can be contested later; licensed survey — boundaries on the ground match the paper; encroachment is more common than first-timers expect. The agreement then fixes price, advance and timelines, with the seller’s identity proof and confirmation the land remains agricultural-classified. Example: The skipped-survey classic: 4 acres bought on paper, 3.7 on the ground — the missing 0.3 under a neighbour’s decades-old bund. The survey that would have caught it costs a few thousand rupees; the shortfall cost lakhs and a boundary case. The process in order Eligibility → verification file → agreement (price, advance, timelines) → registered deed at the SRO with duty and fees → mutation so the record names you. Each step gates the next; hurrying the order is how buyers finance other people’s mistakes. The real total cost Beyond the price: stamp duty and registration (state-set — in Telangana around 7.5% all-in on sale deeds), surveyor’s fees, legal consultation, EC charges — several percentage points above the negotiated figure. Planning to build later? Conversion is a separate application, inspection and state-specific fee again. Red flags Ownership disputes and fraud tied to murky chains; government-allotted / assigned land that cannot legally be resold — including land granted to SC/ST families under protective laws, whose restrictions surface only after payment; unchecked mutation; unsurveyed boundaries. The first two are WALK-AWAY flags; the last two are FIX-FIRST flags. Restricted states vs open states Aspect Agriculturist-restricted states Open-purchase states Who may buy Farming background / eligibility tests required Any buyer Legal source State land-reform law State land-reform law Extra friction Exemption applications, proof of background None on eligibility (ceiling still applies) Suits Active farmers Investors and non-farming buyers NRI restrictions A hard line: NRIs and OCIs cannot purchase agricultural land directly under the exchange-control rules; they CAN inherit it. RBI approval exists in theory, rarely in practice, and leans toward genuine agricultural use. (The full NRI story — funding accounts, repatriation caps — is its own class in this school.) Financing reality Banks lend against farmland more cautiously than against houses — expect more cash upfront, slower sanctions, and a lender re-running your whole verification. Use that: a bank’s refusal is free due diligence naming the defect. Pre-purchase checklist ☐ Eligibility confirmed for the state. ☐ EC and title deed pulled by YOU. ☐ Latest revenue records compared against the deed for name/classification mismatches. ☐ Mutation status verified. ☐ Licensed survey done before the agreement. ☐ Assigned/restricted-origin ruled out. ☐ Full friction cost (duty + fees) priced into the offer. Quick answers (FAQ) Can anyone buy, or only farmers? Depends on the state — Telangana: anyone; several states: restrictions apply. How far back should the history check go? 30 years standard. Can the land be converted later? If zoning allows — a separate process with its own fee. What are the total costs? Price + roughly 7.5% duty/registration (Telangana) + legal, survey and EC costs. Bottom line Agricultural land rewards patience over speed: eligibility, ceiling, chain, record-match, survey — five checks before money, each cheap, each catching a different disaster. The dispute you avoid was always cheaper than the discount you chased. For you: Make the ritual fixed and identical per parcel: portal check → passbook-vs-deed match → EC 30 years → prohibited-list → chain → survey → THEN price. Ritual beats judgement; it has no optimistic days. And each defect found is either a WALK (assigned taint, water-body extent) or a PRICE (pending mutation, survey shortfall) — knowing which bucket instantly is what “experienced” means. ls-rfctlarr: Key Highlights The RFCTLARR Act 2013 (in force 1 Jan 2014) replaced the colonial 1894 acquisition law. Compensation is a FORMULA: market value × rural/urban multiplier, then DOUBLED by a mandatory 100% solatium. Rural land multiplies 1.0–2.0 by distance from the urban centre (some states go higher); urban land sits at 1×. Crops, trees, wells, structures, severance damage and relocation costs are valued and ADDED. R&R benefits — housing, allowances, sometimes jobs or annuities — run alongside the cheque. An award that looks short can be formally challenged — and often is, successfully. What acquisition under RFCTLARR means The state’s power to compulsorily take private land for a public purpose against compensation fixed by law — fundamentally different from a voluntary sale. The 2013 Act was written to make the process humane, participative and transparent after 120 years of complaints about the 1894 law’s arbitrary payouts. It is the law behind every highway, ring road and industrial corridor — including the RRR’s. How compensation is calculated Step 1 — market value (Section 26): the Collector uses registered sale deeds of similar land from the prior three years, taking the HIGHEST of: the top comparable deed, the average of the top half of nearby deeds, or any consented negotiated amount. Step 2 — the multiplier: urban ×1; rural on a sliding 1.0–2.0 scale rising with distance from the urban centre — some states push rural factors higher still. Step 3 — solatium: 100% added on top, doubling the result. Step 4 — additions: structures, wells, trees, standing crops, severance and relocation. Definition — Solatium: a statutory 100% top-up recognising the sale was FORCED. On ₹50 lakh of assessed value it adds another ₹50 lakh — a real break from the 1894 law’s 30% cap. Definition — Severance: when a road takes a strip and leaves your remaining field cut off or oddly shaped, the damage to the REMAINDER is separately compensable — the head owners most often forget to claim. The multiplier bands at a glance Where the land sits Multiplier What that means with solatium Urban land 1.0× (some states allow more) ≈ 2× market value all-in Rural, near the urban centre 1.0–1.5× ≈ 2–3× market value Rural, far from the urban centre Up to 2.0× (higher in some states) ≈ 4× market value — and beyond where states enhance The 12% clock On top of everything, the Collector adds 12% per annum on market value, running from the Social Impact Assessment notification date until the award or possession — whichever comes first. A slow acquisition literally accrues interest for the owner; a mis-tracked SIA date silently underpays it. Rehabilitation and resettlement The Act’s Second Schedule adds a structured R&R package beyond cash: housing, transport and resettlement allowances, and in defined cases employment or annuity support — aimed at restoring livelihoods, not just replacing land value. Crucially it reaches beyond owners: agricultural labourers who worked the acquired fields can qualify without owning an inch. Consent rules for private and PPP projects Where private companies acquire for a public purpose: consent of at least 80% of affected families (70% for public-private partnerships), preceded by a Social Impact Assessment. Emergencies — disasters, critical defence — can invoke the fast-track and skip the SIA. Definition — Social Impact Assessment (SIA): the mandatory study of who is affected and how, done before ordinary acquisitions proceed. Its notification date also starts the 12% clock — a date worth recording the day it appears. Common mistakes in awards The urban multiplier applied to land that should be rural (understating badly); wells, trees and boundary structures skipped because they need a separate survey; the 12% amount miscalculated off the wrong SIA date; and livelihood-dependent families never told they qualify for R&R. None are exotic — all are line-checkable. How to challenge an award An undervalued award is not final because the Collector signed it: apply for a reference to the LARR Authority within the time limit, and appeal onward to the High Court if needed. Most successful challenges trace to exactly the mistakes above — wrong multiplier, missed assets, miscalculated solatium or interest. Check every line before accepting; enhancement is common enough to be a strategy. Example: A Shadnagar-belt farmer’s award used three-year-old registered deeds from a corridor where real prices had doubled — and applied a 1.2 multiplier where distance justified 1.8. Documented recent comparables plus the correct band, argued at reference, materially enhanced the award. The formula is fair; the INPUTS are where owners win or lose. Bottom line The framework is fair on paper; implementation slips are where money leaks — a wrong multiplier here, a missed well there, an SIA that should have happened and did not. Line-by-line checking before acceptance is not distrust; it is how the Act was designed to be used. For you: In the RRR belt every landowner conversation reaches “what if the road takes it?” The developer who can sketch this formula on a napkin — deeds-based value × multiplier + solatium + structures + 12% clock — becomes the most credible person the family has met. And for the land bank: parcels NEAR an alignment appreciate; parcels ON it get the formula — which pays better where registration culture is honest. ls-jda: Key Highlights A JDA trades the owner’s land for a share of what the builder makes of it — neither pays the other upfront. Three sharing structures — area, revenue, profit — each with a different risk profile. Owners typically end with 30–50% of the developed property, set by location and leverage. Courts will not enforce an UNREGISTERED JDA. Registration is existential, not optional. Section 45(5A) defers the owner’s capital gains to the completion-certificate year, not the signing year. Most JDA disasters are builder-selection disasters — vet the builder harder than the draft. What a JDA actually is A structured trade: the owner contributes land — granting development RIGHTS, retaining ownership until later conveyances — and the developer builds at his own cost, returning a slice of the outcome as units or revenue. The owner unlocks idle land without selling; the developer gets prime land without buying. Four laws touch it at once — Contract Act, Transfer of Property Act, Registration Act, RERA — and the Registration Act point is decisive: skip registration and the agreement has no legal teeth at all. The three sharing structures Area sharing (commonest in residential): the built area — carpet, built-up or super built-up, whichever the agreement DEFINES upfront — divides by ratio; 40:60 on 100 flats leaves the owner 40 units to hold, rent or sell, keeping some shelter from a shaky market. Revenue sharing : the developer sells everything and remits the owner’s percentage — cash rather than keys, common in hot urban markets — where the drafting MUST nail gross vs net vs actually-collected, because loose words here breed most fights. Profit sharing : splits what remains after all costs; aligns incentives in theory, but a developer who inflates costs quietly shrinks the owner’s cut — workable only with real audit rights. Definition — Carpet / built-up / super built-up: three ways to measure the same building — usable floor, plus walls, plus common areas. A ratio without a named measure is not a ratio; it is a future argument. Typical ratios and what moves them Location Typical owner share Why Prime Tier-1 corridors 40–50% Scarce, expensive land = owner leverage City periphery 35–45% Land value still strong, competition higher Tier-2 cities 30–40% Land less scarce; builder carries more sales risk Tier-3 / rural fringe 25–35% Developer shoulders nearly all risk Large parcels (5 acres+) swing ratios back toward the owner; higher FSI, residential use, and proximity to existing infrastructure all push the owner’s share up. The professional way to argue any ratio: reverse-engineer it from GDV — owner share ≈ land value ÷ (land value + all-in build cost + builder margin) — then fight over the inputs, not the emotion. How the process runs Negotiate model and ratio → lawyer drafts (sharing clause, timelines, a registered GPA scoped strictly to what the project needs) → REGISTER with the Sub-Registrar → approvals and RERA registration → construction → handover of units or revenue at completion. A mid-sized residential project: three to five years end to end. Red flags in the draft No registration — worthless in court. A bare percentage with no named units, floors or defined revenue base — the single biggest fight-starter. A loosely-drafted GPA handing the developer more authority than the project needs — hard to claw back. No penalty clause — delays go unremedied. No REVERSION clause — a defaulting builder means litigation instead of an automatic handback of development rights. Definition — Reversion clause: the provision that returns development rights to the owner automatically on defined defaults — the difference between a bad year and a decade in court. Insist on it; a builder who resists it is telling you why. Area vs revenue sharing — choosing Area sharing suits owners planning to hold or rent, and shields them somewhat from market swings. Revenue sharing suits owners wanting liquidity who trust the builder’s sales machine. In either: define the measure, the base, and the audit rights in the first schedule — not in a WhatsApp message. Tax implications Section 45(5A) : individual and HUF owners under a REGISTERED JDA pay capital gains in the completion-certificate year, not the signing year — fixing the old horror of owing tax before receiving a single flat. Section 194-IC : cash paid alongside the property share draws 10% TDS. The builder’s own share is stock-in-trade — business income when sold. GST : applies on units sold BEFORE the completion certificate; sales after it are immovable-property sales, GST-exempt — a timing lever both sides should understand. Is the model reliable? The structure holds; the BUILDER is the risk. A developer running out of money leaves a half-built project and a stuck owner. RERA registration, delivery record and financial health, checked before signing, prevent most of what goes wrong later. Before signing — checklist ☐ Builder’s RERA status, delivery record, financial standing verified. ☐ Ratio names exact units / a defined revenue base — never a bare percentage. ☐ GPA scoped tightly to the project. ☐ Penalty clause on missed milestones. ☐ Reversion clause that functions automatically. ☐ Property lawyer AND tax advisor before signature — 45(5A), GST and TDS shape what actually lands in your pocket. Quick answers (FAQ) Is JDA registration mandatory? For enforceability, yes — an unregistered JDA cannot be defended in court. Can the owner cancel on default? With a reversion clause, rights return automatically; without one, litigation. When does the owner pay capital gains? Completion-certificate year, under 45(5A), for registered JDAs. Bottom line A JDA unlocks land value without a sale — and succeeds or fails on two things: the builder’s track record, and drafting that contemplates failure calmly. Registration, a precise sharing clause, and a working reversion clause are the owner’s armour. For you: Your home ground. Walk into every ratio negotiation with the GDV maths done — the side that computed the pie controls the split. Prefer area-sharing when you believe in the corridor more than the counterparty, revenue-sharing when the sales machine is the asset. And the two clauses that keep JDs out of courtrooms: registration immediately, reversion always. Original Deccan Ledger lesson; full source article on 1acre.in (links above). ls-agri-loans: Key Highlights Agricultural land loans are regulated, secured credit under priority-sector lending — not moneylender territory. Farmers, tenant farmers, sharecroppers, SHG members and women applicants all have defined qualifying paths. Banks typically fund 70–85% of valuation at roughly 7–12% a year; tenures can stretch to 15 years. What the bank checks is your land record: deed, RoR, mutation, survey match, valuation, classification. Under interest subvention, prompt repayers on eligible loans can reach an effective ~4%. You do NOT need to already own land — a registered sale agreement on a clean-title plot gets the file moving. What this loan is Secured credit for buying, developing or cultivating farmland, offered under India’s priority-sector framework by public banks, private lenders, NBFCs and regional rural banks. The distinction worth stating plainly: a land purchase loan is a one-time TERM loan secured on the land; a Kisan Credit Card is revolving working capital for crop seasons. Both are “agricultural credit”, which is why they get conflated — but no bank sanctions a land purchase against a KCC limit. Coverage extends to developing fallow land, horticulture and dairying moves, and irrigation or soil improvement on land already owned. What the bank actually verifies Borrower’s capacity — farm records, bank statements or ITRs. Seller’s title — sale deed, Record of Rights, mutation and revenue records. Encumbrances that would block a fresh mortgage. Survey number and boundary matching the paper. An approved valuer’s price. And classification still AGRICULTURAL — reclassified land needs a different product entirely. Definition — Record of Rights (RoR): the state’s core revenue record of who holds each parcel — pattadar passbook in Telangana, 7/12 in Maharashtra, patta in Tamil Nadu. Every bank wants the latest one, whatever the local name. Who can apply RBI priority-sector norms shape it: applicants ~18–65 at maturity; active farmers the default category (a credible farm business plan can work with some lenders); marginal farmers (up to a hectare) often prioritised, small farmers (1–2 ha) eligible; tenant farmers, sharecroppers and landless labourers enter through self-help or joint-liability groups where collective liability replaces collateral; women qualify on equal terms, with several public banks prioritising distress applicants and widows. And you need not own land already — a registered sale agreement on the target plot, with clean seller title, starts the process. Documents you will need Identity (Aadhaar/PAN/Voter ID); address proof; the land file — sale deed, revenue record, survey report; the registered sale agreement; and repayment evidence — bank statements or ITRs. Above ₹3 lakh, add a valuer’s report and legal clearance certificate. The universal requirement under many names: the latest RoR plus updated mutation entries. How the application runs Compare a few nearby lenders → assemble the file BEFORE the branch visit → apply (often online) → the bank verifies documents, inspects the land, orders valuation — larger loans get a legal title search → sanction letter → funds on creation of the mortgage. With clean paper, public banks finish in three to six weeks; unclear land records are the number-one stall. Pitfalls and red flags Survey number not matching ground boundaries — the most common holdup; land quietly reclassified non-agricultural — rules out the product; an undisclosed encumbrance surfacing in the legal search — weeks lost; an UNregistered sale agreement — dead end at most lenders; and chain gaps — the slowest of all to clear. Example: Use the bank as your unpaid second lawyer: even buying with your own cash, run the parcel through a lender’s eyes. A sanction is a quality certificate; a refusal names the defect the seller did not. Rates, amounts, repayment 70–85% of valuation funded; 7–12% yearly by lender and size; tenure to 15 years (7–10 typical); repayment often aligned to harvest cycles rather than flat EMIs; minimal prepayment charges on floating rates; processing fees commonly waived below ₹3 lakh. Government schemes that cut the cost KCC — subsidised revolving credit, useful working capital alongside an acquisition. Modified Interest Subvention — up to ₹3 lakh at a concessional 7%, with a 3% prompt-repayment incentive taking the effective rate to ~4%. RKVY — state-channelled land-development funding. PM Fasal Bima — crop insurance tied to loans, protecting repayment when a season fails. The direction of policy is expansion: agricultural credit targets keep rising year on year. Pre-application checklist ☐ Classification confirmed agricultural in current records. ☐ Survey number and boundaries matching deed AND ground. ☐ Encumbrances, liens, litigation searched. ☐ Sale agreement REGISTERED before it goes to the bank. ☐ 6–12 months of statements / income records assembled. ☐ Subvention eligibility checked before signing. Quick answers (FAQ) Can a first-time farmer get a purchase loan? Yes — eligibility paths exist without prior ownership; the plan and the plot’s paper carry the file. How much will the bank fund? 70–85% of ITS valuation — usually conservative against your negotiated price; budget the gap. What if the survey number mismatches the ground? Fix it before applying; it will stall everything else anyway. Bottom line The loan is accessible and, with schemes, cheaper than it looks. Speed is decided upstream — by the state of the land’s paperwork before the application. Title, survey and encumbrance sorted early turn a three-month file into a three-week one. For you: Financeability is a quality grade on the LAND, not just the borrower — it widens your exit, because your future buyer probably needs the loan even if you never did. Unfinanceable land trades at a structural discount at BOTH ends; price that honestly. Original Deccan Ledger lesson; full source article on 1acre.in (links above). ls-nri-guide: Key Highlights Residential and commercial property: NRIs buy freely — no cap, no RBI approval. Agricultural land, farmhouses and plantations: banned under FEMA, with three narrow exceptions. Repatriating sale money depends on FEMA rules, where the purchase money came from, and tax compliance. Long-term gains (held 24+ months) now taxed at 12.5% WITHOUT indexation — and NRIs miss the grandfathering relief residents got. Buying from abroad is an information problem: due diligence must happen BEFORE the wire, not after. Who counts as an NRI here The definitions run through FEMA, 1999. An NRI is an Indian citizen living abroad — Indian passport overseas. An OCI is a foreign citizen of Indian origin — foreign passport, Indian roots. For property purchases the two follow essentially identical rules, so everything below applies to both. What NRIs can and cannot buy Freely: apartments, villas, houses, offices, shops — residential and commercial, any number, no RBI approval. Never: agricultural land, farmhouses, plantation property — a national ban, whatever the buyer’s income or country, and it covers every route: sale deed, agreement to sell, or any indirect structure trying to dress the purchase up. Why the farmland ban exists The restriction lives in FEMA’s capital-account framework — today the Non-debt Instruments Rules, 2019 plus the RBI Master Direction, not one neat section. The policy logic: farmland touches food security, and offshore money flooding in could distort prices and displace the people who actually work the land. RBI approval technically exists but is granted rarely, for genuine agricultural or public-interest cases — it is not an investment route. And breaking the rule is not a slap on the wrist: the transaction can be VOIDED, the Enforcement Directorate can step in, and penalties can reach three times the value. The three exceptions Inheritance — the common path: an NRI can inherit farmland from a resident Indian (or from another NRI with RBI clearance), and can later sell it — but only to a resident Indian. Gift from a specified relative — allowed if the giver is a RESIDENT Indian who qualifies as a specified relative under FEMA; NRI-to-NRI farmland gifting is barred. Prior ownership — farmland you owned while resident stays yours after your status changes; the ban bites only on NEW acquisitions. In all three cases, sending the eventual sale money abroad is not automatic — RBI guidance and tax compliance govern it. The buying process, step by step 1) Confirm eligibility — your NRI/OCI status, and that the property is residential/commercial, not agricultural or plantation. 2) Shortlist RERA-registered projects and verify approvals with the authority. 3) Due diligence — 30-year title search plus EC, ruling out disputes, mortgages and legally non-transferable land. 4) Open the NRI account — NRE, NRO or FCNR; every rupee routes through it (cash is barred under FEMA and tax law alike). 5) Execute a PoA if you will not attend — embassy-attested or apostilled in Hague-convention countries, then stamped in India before use. 6) Sign the agreement on stamp paper with a payment schedule; register within four months. 7) Transfer funds and KEEP the Foreign Inward Remittance Certificate. 8) Pay stamp duty at the state’s rate. 9) Register the sale deed — in person or via the PoA holder — this is the ownership proof. 10) Afterwards: file tax on any rent, and keep records seven years. Definition — NRE / NRO / FCNR: the three NRI bank accounts. NRE holds foreign earnings (fully repatriable), NRO holds Indian earnings (repatriation capped), FCNR holds foreign-currency deposits. WHICH account funded the purchase decides how freely the sale money can leave later. Repatriation — getting money out later From an NRO account, up to USD 1 million per financial year can go abroad, subject to tax compliance. Property bought with FOREIGN funds via NRE: full repatriation of sale proceeds, for up to two residential properties; beyond two, the money joins the USD-1-million pipeline. Bought with NRO (India-earned) money: capped and paperwork-heavy. The lesson runs backwards in time: the repatriation freedom you want at EXIT is decided by the account you use at ENTRY. Example: Two NRIs each sell a Hyderabad flat for ₹2 crore. One bought via NRE with dollars — proceeds wire out cleanly. The other bought with NRO rupees — the same money now queues under the annual cap with Forms 15CA/15CB. Identical flats; the funding route made the difference. Documents you will need Identity: passport (with OCI card if applicable), PAN, proof of overseas residence. Property: title deed with 30-year history, EC, regulatory approvals, and for completed buildings the approved plan and occupancy certificate. Transaction: NRI-account statements, the FIRC, the attested PoA if buying in absentia, and Forms 15CA/15CB where remittances abroad cross ₹5 lakh a year. Tax obligations TDS turns on who SELLS: buy from a resident and TDS is the small 1% over ₹50 lakh; buy from another NRI and TDS applies at much higher rates regardless of value. Capital gains: property held over 24 months is long-term, taxed at 12.5% — and NRIs do NOT get the grandfathered indexation relief residents kept, so old purchases can carry surprisingly large taxable gains. Rent earned in India is taxed in India (standard deduction applies); tax treaties usually let you credit Indian tax against the home-country bill. Buying from a distance — the real risk The hardest part of absentee buying is the gap between what a listing claims and what the land is. Map overlays and verified survey numbers narrow that gap — classification, zoning, boundary, location — before you wire an advance or fly in. But no map reads a title chain, catches a forged deed, or gives FEMA and tax advice: a property lawyer and a tax advisor who handle NRI transactions remain non-negotiable, because a wrong classification does not just lose money — it can void the transaction. Quick answers (FAQ) Can an NRI buy restricted or assigned land? No — the assigned-land bans apply on top of FEMA. Any cap on how many properties? No cap on residential/commercial ownership; repatriation rules differ beyond two. Buy without visiting India? Yes — via a properly attested and stamped PoA. Sell inherited farmland? Yes, but only to a resident Indian. What if an NRI buys farmland in breach? Transaction voidable, ED proceedings, penalty up to 3× the value. Bottom line The rules are clear on paper and unforgiving in practice. Confirm the land’s classification BEFORE committing, route every payment through the right NRI account, and put a lawyer and tax advisor on the file — the two costs that are always cheaper than the mistake. For you: NRI money is a major buyer pool for Hyderabad plots — and every NRI buyer’s first fear is exactly this lesson. A venture that hands NRI buyers a ready file (residential classification proof, RERA number, PoA template, TDS guidance) converts that fear into sales. Also: never let a broker pitch your FARM plots to NRI buyers — that deal voids itself. Original Deccan Ledger lesson; full source article on 1acre.in (links above). ls-scams: Key Highlights Fraud thrives where records are scattered: ~95% of RoRs are computerised, but only ~68% of cadastral maps. The deadliest scam is the LEGAL-LOOKING one: registered deeds on assigned land are void — registration proves nothing. Seven patterns cover most of the market: forged titles, restricted land, duplicate sales, PoA abuse, encroachment, benami, fake pre-launch schemes. The defence is always the same: pull the records YOURSELF — RoR, EC, prohibited list, title chain. Remote buyers and absentee owners are the favourite targets. Why India’s land market attracts so much fraud Fraud grows wherever information is scarce and checking is hard. India’s records are digitising UNEVENLY — about 95% of Records of Rights computerised but only 68% of cadastral maps, with some districts still on ageing paper — and every state runs its own system. The favourite victims: buyers unfamiliar with local revenue records, people purchasing remotely, and plots whose owners are absent or unaware something is being sold in their name. The most devastating one: restricted land sold as normal Certain land legally CANNOT be freely sold: government-assigned land, tribal land, ceiling-surplus land, endowment (temple) land, forest land. The scam: a legitimate-looking registered document, payment made, registration completed — and years or decades later the government reclaims the land because it was assigned all along. Buyer loses land, money and everything built on it. The legal trap: the prohibited-list mechanism (Section 22-A) only BLOCKS registration of parcels actually on the Collector’s list — unlisted assigned parcels register fine — but the transfer-ban law voids the sale regardless of what any registrar accepted. So: check the prohibited register AND the revenue record’s remarks, always. Seven scams to know 1) Title fraud and forged documents — the most widespread: a fraudster forges papers, poses as owner or PoA holder, sells land that is not theirs; forged paper carries zero legal weight, which is why the CHAIN matters more than the current deed. 2) Restricted-land sales — as above. 3) Duplicate sales — one plot sold to two or more buyers, exploiting slow registration; not a pure first-to-register race (a deed relates back to its execution date under Section 47), but the genuinely prior sale usually prevails and everyone else litigates. 4) PoA abuse — forged, expired or revoked PoAs used to sell without the owner’s knowledge; an unregistered PoA, or one not clearly authorising sale, is a warning. 5) Encroachment folded in — the boundary shown quietly includes government or neighbouring land; good title to part, nothing on the rest; a boundary survey catches it. 6) Benami deals — property in someone else’s name to hide the real buyer; illegal under the 2016 Benami law, with confiscation and up to seven years’ rigorous imprisonment. 7) Fake pre-launch schemes — units sold in unapproved projects with assured-return promises backed by post-dated cheques that bounce; RERA bars selling before registration, so a pre-launch pitch WITHOUT a RERA number is the tell. Definition — Benami transaction: a purchase held in a name-lender’s name while someone else pays and controls it. Since the 2016 amendment the property can be confiscated outright — buyer-side participation is itself the crime. Red flags and what they mean Warning sign What it usually means What to do Price well below market Defect the seller knows and you don’t Slow down; the discount IS the disclosure Pressure to close fast Verification window being shortened deliberately Never pay before checks complete Seller supplies all documents, resists your own EC pull Papers may be curated or forged Pull EC and RoR yourself from official sources Sale via PoA, owner unreachable Possible PoA abuse or a dead/unaware principal Meet or video-verify the owner; check PoA registration “Registration will fix everything” Confusing registration with valid title Remember: void transfers register too No RERA number on a project pitch Unapproved / pre-launch scheme Verify on the state RERA portal before any token Documents to check before any purchase ☐ Title + sale deed — seller’s name matches the record; chain traced 30 years. ☐ Record of Rights — owner, classification, mutation history, restriction remarks. ☐ EC — pulled by YOU from the sub-registrar; never the seller’s copy. ☐ Land use / conversion — classification confirmed; conversion completed if it was agricultural. ☐ Mutation — updated, no restriction notes. ☐ Tax receipts — dues attach to the LAND, not the old owner. ☐ RERA — verified on the portal for any plotted or builder project. ☐ PoA, if involved — authorises sale, registered where required, traceable to the real owner. What maps can and cannot catch Survey-number maps, master-plan overlays and satellite imagery catch boundary and zoning mismatches — whether the parcel’s ground reality matches the deed, and whether it sits in a restricted zone — before a site visit. They cannot read a title chain, tell a forged deed from a genuine one, or check the prohibited list. That work stays with the sub-registrar’s records and a revenue-law advocate. Quick answers (FAQ) Most common scam? Title fraud with forged documents. How do I know if land has transfer restrictions? RoR remarks + the state’s prohibited-property register. Can I buy through a PoA? Yes, with independent verification of the PoA and the principal — PoA sales are not inherently illegitimate. What if I unknowingly bought restricted land? The transfer is void; get a revenue advocate immediately. Is RERA-registered land always safe? Safer — but RERA checks the project, not the title chain; do both. How to report fraud? Police complaint (EOW for large frauds) + civil suit; registration of a case does not undo the transfer, so prevention is the real remedy. Bottom line Nearly every land scam succeeds at the same moment: when the buyer accepts someone else’s paperwork instead of pulling their own. RoR, EC, prohibited list, 30-year chain, boundary survey — five self-service checks defeat all seven scams. For you: Your buyers fear exactly this list — which makes it your marketing. A venture that publishes its own verification file (chain, EC, prohibited-list clearance, DTCP approval) sells trust the unorganised market cannot. Internally: rule — no landowner conversation advances until the RoR and prohibited-list check are done, however warm the introduction. ls-assigned-land: Key Highlights Assigned land = government surplus/wasteland granted to landless poor families for cultivation or house sites — possession and use, NOT free ownership. Transfers are prohibited or void under state land-reform laws; a registered sale deed changes nothing. The government can RESUME the land at any time, with no compensation to the buyer — and buying it can carry up to six months’ jail. Narrow exceptions: inheritance by heirs, bank mortgages, and good-faith pre-Act purchases by landless poor persons. The whole defence is two checks: the revenue record’s remarks and the Section 22-A prohibited list. What assigned land is Government surplus or wasteland handed to landless poor persons — typically agricultural labourers or SC/ST families — for cultivation or as a house site, under land-reform and welfare schemes. What transfers is possession and limited use rights; ownership stays CONDITIONAL with the state. The condition that matters to every buyer: the grant usually prohibits sale. Why the law bans its sale The point of assignment is welfare — land in the hands of the landless. If assignees could sell, the poor would be bought out for quick cash and the policy would defeat itself; so state laws (in Telangana, the Assigned Lands (Prohibition of Transfers) Act) bar selling, gifting, leasing or otherwise transferring without government permission, and declare violating transfers invalid. What “void ab initio” means Treated as if the transaction never legally happened — no title passes, ever. Even land that changed hands TEN times through ten registered deeds: every link is equally invalid. A registered document does not make you the owner here; the paper has no legal weight at all. One narrow protection exists: a landless poor person who bought in good faith, for value, from the original assignee BEFORE the Act commenced and was in possession on that date — it protects the poor, not an investor. Definition — Void ab initio: void “from the beginning” — not cancelled later, but never valid at any moment. Nothing downstream of it can be valid either. What happens if it is sold anyway The government can resume the land at ANY time — no limitation period runs in its favour going away — and reassign it to another eligible landless family. The buyer gets no compensation; no civil court can decree the sale into existence. And the consequence sellers never mention: acquiring assigned land in breach of the prohibition is an OFFENCE carrying up to six months’ imprisonment. The buyer is not just a victim in this law’s eyes. Transferability by land category Category Freely transferable? Notes Patta (private) land Yes Ordinary sale deed + registration Assigned land No Transfer void; resumption + penal risk Tribal-area land Highly restricted Transfers to non-tribals barred in scheduled areas Ceiling-surplus land No Vested in government for redistribution Endowment (temple) land No Alienation needs statutory sanction, rarely given Forest land No Central law bars de-reservation without approval What an assignee CAN do Cultivate for the family; pass the land to legal heirs (inheritance is generally not a prohibited transfer); mortgage it to a scheduled bank, co-operative or notified institution — the one security the Act permits; build a house where the assignment was a house site. And in some states, apply to the Collector for DE-RESTRICTION — converting it into regular patta land eligible for sale once eligibility conditions are met. Rules vary; the revenue authority’s word is the only one that counts. How to check whether a plot is assigned Pull the latest Record of Rights from the state revenue department and read the REMARKS column for “assigned”, “granted” or restriction notes. Check the state’s prohibited-property register (Section 22-A list) for the survey number. Ask the local revenue office directly. And read the original ASSIGNMENT ORDER — it states plainly whether transfer is prohibited. Fifteen minutes of record-reading is the difference between owning land and owning a legal dead end. Example: The classic Hyderabad-belt trap: a corridor plot at 40% below market, seller waving a registered deed from a 2009 purchase. The RoR remarks column reads “asgd”. That deed — and the one before it — are both void; the discount was the disclosure. Walk away; no lawyer can cure it. If you are the assignee wanting to sell Apply to the competent revenue authority for removal of the transfer restriction where state law permits, BEFORE entering any agreement. For SC/ST or tribal-origin land, confirm whether Collector approval is mandatory. Selling first and regularising later is not a sequence the law recognises. Quick answers (FAQ) Can assigned land be sold after N years? No automatic ripening — only formal de-restriction changes its status. Why do registered deeds exist on assigned land? Because registration only blocks parcels actually on the prohibited list; the registrar’s stamp never validates a void transfer. Can family inherit it? Yes — heirs succeed; that is not a prohibited transfer. Can it be mortgaged? Only to banks/institutions the Act permits. Can it ever become freehold? In some states, via Collector-approved conversion to patta land. Bottom line Assigned land is the one category where late homework has NO remedy — no cure, no compensation, no sympathetic court. The RoR remarks and the 22-A list, checked before any money moves, are the entire safeguard. For you: For a plotting developer this is the first gate on every parcel — before price, before layout dreams: Dharani/RoR remarks + 22-A check on each survey number. One assigned survey number inside an assembled venture can poison the whole layout’s marketability. Make the check a fixed line item in your acquisition template. ls-crz: Key Highlights CRZ rules control construction near the coastline — they decide whether a coastal plot is buildable at all. Four zones: CRZ-I (ecologically sensitive — essentially no building), II (urban coast), III (rural coast), IV (the water itself). The 2019 notification cut the rural No Development Zone from 200 m to 50 m in dense villages — but ONLY once the state’s Coastal Zone Management Plan is approved under it; until then 200 m continues. Every coastal project needs PRIOR clearance — courts have ordered completed buildings demolished for lacking it. Distance is measured from the officially demarcated High Tide Line, not the visible waterline. What the CRZ is and why it exists The Coastal Regulation Zone is the legal strip along India’s coastline within which activity is controlled — notified under the Environment (Protection) Act, 1986, with the central environment ministry as nodal authority and state Coastal Zone Management Authorities enforcing. The balance it strikes: protecting mangroves, wetlands and dunes, protecting fishing communities’ livelihoods, and still allowing coastal development — by classifying the coast into zones, each with its own rules on construction, industry and land conversion near the high tide line. Definition — High Tide Line (HTL): the officially DEMARCATED line the sea reaches at highest tide — mapped by authorised agencies, not eyeballed from the beach. Every setback measures from this line; measuring from the visible waterline is the classic buyer error. The four zones CRZ-I — ecologically sensitive: IA covers mangroves and coral reefs, IB the intertidal strip between tide lines; new construction essentially off the table, narrow exceptions for defence, atomic energy and major public infrastructure. CRZ-II — urban coast: already-developed municipal coastline; building allowed only LANDWARD of existing roads or authorised structures — never toward the sea — following local FSI/FAR. CRZ-III — rural coast, split by density (Census 2011): IIIA is dense rural coast (>2,161 people/sq km) with a 50-metre No Development Zone; IIIB is sparse coast at 200 metres. CRZ-IV — the water: IVA open sea from low tide line to 12 nautical miles, IVB tidal inland waters; traditional fishing protected, untreated discharge banned. Definition — No Development Zone (NDZ): the strip inland from the HTL where new construction is barred regardless of ownership. Owning land inside the NDZ means owning a view, not a building site. Zones at a glance Zone What it covers Building position CRZ-IA / IB Mangroves, reefs / intertidal strip Essentially none (defence & major public works excepted) CRZ-II Developed urban coast Landward of existing road/structure line only; local FSI applies CRZ-IIIA Dense rural coast (>2,161/km²) Beyond 50 m NDZ — once the state’s CZMP is approved; 200 m until then CRZ-IIIB Sparse rural coast Beyond 200 m NDZ CRZ-IVA / IVB Sea to 12 nm / tidal inland waters No construction; fishing protected, discharge banned What changed in 2019 Three big moves. The long-standing FREEZE on Floor Space Index in eligible coastal areas was lifted — development can follow local planning regulations, subject to CRZ conditions. Clearances were DECENTRALISED — state authorities now handle much more, with the centre appraising specified categories. And the rural NDZ was cut for dense villages — but here is the catch buyers miss: the relaxations take effect only after the state’s Coastal Zone Management Plan prepared under the 2019 framework is formally approved. Until that approval, the OLD setbacks continue. A “50-metre plot” in a state with an unapproved CZMP is still a 200-metre plot. Definition — Coastal Zone Management Plan (CZMP): the state’s official map of its coast — which stretch is which zone, where the HTL runs. The 2019 relaxations are switched on, state by state, only by its approval. What is permanently off-limits Whatever the zone: new industries, hazardous-substance storage, sand and coral mining, land reclamation and bunding within the regulated distance. Groundwater: no extraction within 200 m of the HTL except community use; between 200 and 500 m, only manual drawing from ordinary wells, and only where no alternative exists. Getting clearance Mandatory BEFORE any construction in the zone. Jurisdiction splits by category: CRZ-I and IV go to the central ministry; CRZ-II and III — covering most residential and commercial work — to the State CZMA. Small mercy for individuals: self-dwelling units up to 300 sq m get a simpler path through the local authority. Building without clearance is the one shortcut with a documented ending: courts have ordered COMPLETED buildings demolished. Example: A buyer takes a “beach-view villa plot” 120 m from the water in a dense fishing village, told “the new rules allow 50 m”. The state’s CZMP is still pending approval — so the 200 m NDZ applies, and the plot cannot host a villa at all. The seller quoted the notification; the buyer needed the CZMP status. Before you buy or build near the coast ☐ Confirm which CRZ regime applies to the EXACT survey number. ☐ Check whether the state’s CZMP is approved under CRZ 2019 — this decides 50 m vs 200 m. ☐ Measure from the demarcated HTL, not the waterline. ☐ Identify the clearance authority (central vs state) for that zone. ☐ Obtain a certified CZMP extract for the survey number. ☐ Engage a lawyer experienced in coastal regulation before money moves. Quick answers (FAQ) Minimum distance from the sea to build a house? Zone-dependent: 50 m in approved dense rural stretches, 200 m otherwise in rural coast, road-line rule in urban CRZ-II. Is the 50 m NDZ automatic? No — only after CZMP approval. Hotels and resorts? Possible in permitted stretches with clearance, never inside the NDZ or CRZ-I. Building without clearance? Fines, prosecution — and demolition orders that survive completion. Bottom line On the coast, the zone IS the value: the same acre is a resort site in CRZ-II, a 200-metre wait in IIIB, and a permanent no in CRZ-I. Verify zone, CZMP status and HTL for the exact survey number before believing any price. For you: Hyderabad money loves Vizag, Goa and ECR beach plots — when that pitch reaches you or your investors, the three questions are: which zone exactly, is the state’s CZMP approved, and where is the demarcated HTL? No certified answer, no advance. The same discipline you apply to Dharani at home applies to the CZMP at the beach. Original Deccan Ledger lesson; full source article on 1acre.in (links above). ls-boundary: Key Highlights Most boundary fights trace to outdated surveys, vague old deeds, or inherited land split informally without fresh measurement. Cadastral maps and Field Measurement Books carry more weight in these disputes than any other evidence. A fresh official survey from the revenue department is the FIRST move, not the last resort. Twelve years of open hostile possession can ripen into adverse possession — delay has a price in land, not just time. Digitisation is real but uneven: ~95% of RoRs computerised, ~68% of maps, geo-referencing at ~49%. Why these disputes keep happening Outdated or inconsistent records; ambiguous boundary descriptions in older sale deeds; inherited property subdivided informally without fresh surveys; delayed mutation. Many records originate in the colonial era, and though the national modernisation drive (DILRMP) has digitised much, progress is uneven — leaving some areas running on decades-old measurements while land prices around them multiplied. Survey records: where every resolution starts Two records outrank everything else. The cadastral map — the official parcel map identifying each survey number and its neighbours. The Field Measurement Book (FMB) — the recorded measurements from official surveys of each parcel. Together with title documents and revenue records, these are what authorities and courts use to determine where one property legally ends and the next begins — and they beat personal recollections and “the old tamarind tree” descriptions every time. Definition — Field Measurement Book (FMB): the survey department’s measurement sketch of a single survey number — sides, angles, extent. In a boundary fight it is the closest thing to ground truth on paper. The resolution playbook, step by step 1) Assemble your papers — sale deed, mutation entries, tax receipts, old photographs; download the RoR from the state portal; and FIRST check that the survey number on your deed matches the Record of Rights — a mismatch there gets fixed before anything else. 2) Apply for an official government survey — a certified surveyor measures and marks the actual boundary on site; the report becomes central evidence in any later proceeding. 3) Talk first — holding a government survey report changes the conversation from your word against theirs to a neutral document; direct dialogue and state mediation services resolve more than people expect. 4) Legal notice — if the survey supports you, a notice puts your position on record and signals escalation. 5) Revenue authority or civil court — a permanent injunction (Specific Relief Act, s.38) stops ongoing encroachment; a declaratory suit (s.34) establishes ownership and fixes the line; a possession suit recovers taken land. Courts often appoint a local commissioner (CPC Order XXVI Rule 9) to measure and report — influential, though weighed with all the other evidence. Resolution routes compared Route Needs Produces Time Official survey + negotiation Survey fee, both parties talking Marked boundary, often a settlement Weeks–months Mediation Willingness; state mediation services Recorded compromise Months Revenue proceedings Survey report, revenue records Administrative demarcation orders Months Civil suit (injunction / declaration / possession) Advocate, full evidence, court fees Binding decree; commissioner’s measurement Years What digitisation has (and has not) changed Less than the headlines suggest. About 95% of RoRs are computerised — the TEXT record is usually a download. But cadastral maps sit at ~68%, geo-referencing at ~49%, only 11 states/UTs have finished map digitisation, and ULPIN covers a bit over 30% of parcels. Meaning: the record that MATTERS in a boundary fight — the map — is precisely the one most likely to still need verification at the local revenue office. Cross-check every digital map against the official survey record before relying on it. The clock you cannot ignore Twelve years of open, hostile, continuous possession can EXTINGUISH your title through adverse possession — and a suit for possession based on title carries the same twelve-year limitation. An encroachment tolerated politely for a decade is quietly becoming the neighbour’s land. Acting early is not aggression; it is how the limitation law forces you to behave. Example: A family “adjusts” with a neighbour’s shed two metres over the line for fifteen years, then sells — and the buyer’s survey triggers the fight. By then the neighbour’s adverse-possession clock has already run. The survey that cost a few thousand rupees in year one would have settled it while it was still a shed, not a claim. What to do (and avoid) during a dispute DO: pull RoR and cadastral map, confirm deed-vs-record survey number, file for the official survey at the Tehsildar’s office, negotiate with the report in hand, then notice, then court — asking for a commissioner when you get there. AVOID: self-help demolition or fence-moving (it converts your civil case into their criminal complaint), oral settlements with nothing recorded, and waiting out of politeness while the twelve-year clock runs. Quick answers (FAQ) Most reliable evidence? The cadastral map and FMB, plus a fresh official survey. Can maps hold up in court? Yes — weighed with title documents and other evidence. Survey doesn’t match my deed? Fix the record mismatch first; it undermines everything downstream. Can my neighbour claim my land by occupying it? After twelve years of open hostile possession — yes. Check records online? Text records usually; maps often still need the revenue office. Bottom line Boundary fights are won on certified measurements, not memories. Survey early, record everything, act inside the limitation clock — and treat the few-thousand-rupee survey as the cheapest insurance land ownership offers. For you: For a plotting developer boundaries are the product itself — every plot you sell is a promise about a line. Fresh FMB-matched survey BEFORE layout design, stones planted and photographed at handover, and the survey report in each buyer’s file: that ritual is why organised ventures command premiums over the neighbour selling “by the tree line”. ls-poa-rules: Key Highlights A PoA authorises someone to ACT for you — sign, register, manage, negotiate. It can never hand over ownership. Suraj Lamp (Supreme Court, 2011) settled it: a PoA is not a title-transfer instrument; Shakeel Ahmed (2023) confirmed old GPA chains get no pass. A PoA normally DIES with the principal (Section 201) — except where the agent holds a real interest in the property (Section 202). Registration is mandatory whenever a PoA creates an interest in land, is marked irrevocable, or empowers sale/gift/transfer. Stamp duty turns on the relationship: close family pay nominal rates; unrelated buyers/developers face conveyance-level charges. What a PoA actually does for land One person — the principal — authorises another — the agent — to act on their behalf: signing agreements, handling Sub-Registrar paperwork, managing tenants, negotiating a sale. Representative authority only. The persistent confusion is treating a PoA as a stand-in for a sale — it is not and cannot be: under Section 54 of the Transfer of Property Act, only a REGISTERED SALE DEED transfers title to immovable property. GPA vs SPA: picking the instrument A General PoA grants sweeping authority — suited to an NRI overseeing property across years and distance, but broad authority is hard to police, and if the agent oversteps, the very breadth makes the overstep harder to prove. A Special PoA is built for ONE job and expires when it is done. For land, advocates lean SPA: narrow scope, less room for misuse, cleaner record. What the Supreme Court has said Suraj Lamp (2011) : the “GPA sale” — the once-common practice of selling property via GPA + agreement + will, skipping the sale deed and its stamp duty — transfers NO title. Shakeel Ahmed (2023) : confirmed the principle applies to old chains too — decades-old GPA transactions do not ripen into ownership with time. If your seller’s ownership story runs through a GPA instead of a registered deed, there is no ownership in the story. Example: A Shamshabad plot is offered cheap: the “owner” bought it in 2008 “on GPA” from the recorded owner and has possession ever since. Under Suraj Lamp he owns nothing — only the recorded owner (or their heirs) can convey. The fix, if everyone is alive and willing: a proper registered sale deed from the true owner now, with duty paid. Without that, the plot is unbuyable at any discount. The five classic PoA risks 1) Revoked but presented as valid — an unregistered cancellation shows no outward sign, so a revoked PoA can still deceive a third party. 2) Death of the principal — agency ends automatically under Section 201; anything signed after is void — except the narrow Section 202 case where the agent holds a genuine interest in the property itself. 3) Tangled chains of sub-authority — each PoA granting power to the next makes true ownership harder to trace; buyers inherit disputes they never saw. 4) Self-dealing — an agent selling to HIMSELF is valid only if the PoA explicitly permits it; otherwise a breach of fiduciary duty. 5) Missing registration — where a PoA permits sale, gift or transfer, registration at the sub-registrar is not optional; skipping it guts the document’s standing. Definition — Section 202 (Contract Act): the exception that makes a PoA survive the principal’s death: when the agent has a real INTEREST in the property (say, money already advanced against it), the authority is coupled with that interest and does not lapse. Everything else dies with the principal. Registration, stamp duty, validity Registration is mandatory when the PoA creates an interest in land, is marked irrevocable, or empowers sale/gift/transfer; a PoA limited to rent collection follows lighter rules. Stamp duty follows the relationship : close family typically nominal; an unrelated buyer or developer holding a sale-empowering PoA can face conveyance-level duty — precisely to kill the GPA-sale dodge. NRIs : execute before the Indian mission (or apostille in Hague-convention countries) and stamp within three months of the document reaching India. How to verify a land PoA before acting on it ☐ The PoA names the exact survey number, the exact act, and a duration. ☐ Registered, where the sale/irrevocable/interest test applies. ☐ A revocation clause built in from day one. ☐ The principal INDEPENDENTLY confirmed as owner — in the state land record, not the PoA’s own recitals. ☐ The principal confirmed ALIVE (for a Section 201 document, this is not a formality). ☐ EC pulled — showing any PoA, mortgage or transaction already registered against the parcel. ☐ The land itself transferable — no assigned/prohibited/acquisition taint, because no PoA overrides a land-law restriction. Quick answers (FAQ) Can a PoA be used to SELL land? An agent under a valid, registered, sale-empowering PoA can EXECUTE a sale deed for the owner — but the PoA itself never makes anyone an owner. Does calling it “irrevocable” make it irrevocable? No — the label doesn’t; only a genuine Section 202 interest does. What if the principal dies? Authority ends; post-death signatures are void (Section 202 excepted). Stamp duty? Relationship-dependent — nominal for close family, conveyance-level for unrelated sale-empowered holders. Bottom line A PoA is a tool for ACTING at a distance, not for owning. Verify the principal, the registration, the scope and the land’s own transferability — and treat any ownership chain that runs through a GPA as a chain with a missing link. For you: Two rules for your desk. Buying: any parcel whose chain contains a “GPA sale” is unpriced risk — either the true owner signs a fresh registered deed or you pass. Structuring your own JDs: the development GPA you take from landowners should be SPECIAL, scoped to the project, registered, with the JDA’s reversion clause mirrored in it — broad GPAs frighten landowners and courts alike. ls-agri-to-resi: Key Highlights Agricultural land must usually be CONVERTED before residential construction is legal on it. Approval depends on the master plan, zoning and state land-use law — not on willingness to pay. Green belts, protected agricultural zones, forests and environmentally restricted land often cannot be converted at any price. The order comes from the competent planning or revenue authority, with documents and a site inspection. Buying land “already converted”? Verify the order is VALID and unexpired — a lapsed conversion reverts the land to agricultural. Agricultural vs residential land: the real difference Agricultural land is meant for farming, and its registration, taxation and transfer rules all follow from that purpose. Converted land costs more per square yard — but it carries the legal standing you need to build, raise a home loan, or sell to someone who will. The premium is not decoration; it is the difference between a plot and a field. What the law actually requires Start with the MASTER PLAN, not the application form — this is where most people get the sequence backwards. Formal conversion approval from the competent planning or revenue authority is required before agricultural land can legally host residential construction, and that approval must align with the master plan zone, the zoning classification, and the state’s land-revenue statutes. Two hard truths follow: where the plan already designates the land residential, conversion is not discretionary — it should be granted; where the plan marks the zone green belt, forest or agriculture-protection, conversion is simply NOT AVAILABLE. No fee fixes a blocking zone. Definition — Master plan: the government’s long-term land-use map for a region — which areas are residential, commercial, industrial, green. In conversion matters it outranks everything: the plan decides what is possible; the application only executes it. Documents you will need ☐ Title deed and the 30-year chain of title. ☐ Updated land-record extract — registered deed, 7/12, patta, or your state’s equivalent (pattadar passbook in Telangana). ☐ Survey sketch, master plan extract, and an EC. ☐ NOCs from agriculture, town planning, forest or water-resources departments where applicable. Getting the file right the FIRST time saves months of back-and-forth. The step-by-step process 1) Pull the master plan extract; confirm the zone permits residential use. 2) File the application with the revenue or planning authority for your state and zone. 3) Pay the conversion fee — assessed on area, location and proposed use. 4) Site inspection: an official verifies the land matches the application. 5) Receive the conversion order; the land record is updated. 6) READ THE CONDITIONS on pages two and three — they decide whether the order stays alive. 7) Apply for building-plan sanction from the local body before any construction starts — conversion permits the USE; the sanction permits the BUILDING. Common challenges The zone itself blocking the change — no application can convert green-belt, forest or protection-zone land. Delays or rejection from incomplete files, missing NOCs, or mismatches found at inspection. And the quiet one: conversion orders that LAPSE because construction timelines or conditions went unmet — leaving the land agricultural despite a framed approval on the wall. Example: A buyer pays a premium for a “converted” plot with a 2019 order. Condition 4 on page two required construction to commence within three years; nothing was built. The order lapsed in 2022 — the parcel is agricultural again, and the premium bought paper. One reading of the conditions would have repriced the deal. Best practices before you start Master plan zone first; then road access, water and soil. A short consultation with a local surveyor costs less than discovering a blocking issue after the fee is paid. And engage someone who knows THAT district’s revenue office — procedures genuinely differ between neighbouring districts. Quick answers (FAQ) Is conversion mandatory before building a house? Generally yes — building on unconverted agricultural land invites demolition and denies you sanction, loans and clean resale. Who approves? The competent revenue or planning authority (RDO/Collector-side in Telangana, with HMDA/DTCP layers for layouts). Can any land be converted if I pay? No — the zone decides; money cannot move a green belt. Does an order expire? Yes — it is conditional and time-bound; verify validity when buying “converted” land. Can NRIs apply? For land they lawfully hold (e.g. inherited) — subject to the same zoning rules. If I skip conversion? Unauthorised use: penalties, demolition risk, no sanction, and a discount when you sell. Bottom line Conversion is a sequence, not a fee: zone first, statute second, payment last — and the order you receive is a living document with conditions and an expiry. Read it like a contract, because it is one. For you: This is the machinery of your margin: farmland in, NA/DTCP-approved plots out. Your edge is the SEQUENCE discipline — verify the master-plan zone before the land is even priced, and when buying “converted” parcels from others, audit the order’s conditions and dates like a bank would. ls-mutation: Key Highlights Mutation updates the owner’s name in the government’s revenue register after sale, inheritance, gift or partition — it does NOT transfer ownership; registration did that. Skipping it is a top reason buyers fight tax notices and loan rejections years after a purchase. The name changes by state — dakhil kharij, intiqal, patta transfer, khata transfer — the process is the same. A DISPUTED claim cannot be mutated by a revenue officer: it goes to civil court first. The Supreme Court’s position cuts both ways: mutation is not proof of title — but its ABSENCE is proof something was never finished. What mutation is The update of the government’s revenue register to show the CURRENT owner’s name after a sale, inheritance, gift or partition. It is different from the sale deed and registration: mutation affects the tax and revenue record and does not by itself prove legal title. Rural land mutates at the revenue office; urban property at the municipal corporation. The application typically needs the sale deed, previous mutation records and identity proof — and it matters for paying property tax under the right name, and for every future loan or resale. Definition — Mutation (dakhil kharij / khata transfer / patta transfer): the state updating its own ledger of who holds the land — the bridge between the registered deed and the revenue record. Registration changes OWNERSHIP; mutation changes the government’s BOOKS. What the process verifies Not a rubber stamp. The reviewing officer checks that the applicant is the rightful new owner based on a valid transfer document — sale deed, gift deed, or inheritance record — and cross-checks the property’s survey number, area and boundaries against the existing revenue record. What the exercise CANNOT do: establish or guarantee title. It aligns the ledger; it does not adjudicate ownership — which is why a disputed claim goes to civil court, not the Tehsildar. Documents by route How the land came to you Core document for mutation Purchase Registered sale deed Gift Registered gift deed Inheritance (no will) Death certificate + legal-heir certificate Inheritance (will) Death certificate + will (probate where applicable) Partition Registered partition deed / decree Most state portals also want the latest tax receipt and identity proof, whatever the route. One heir applying while others exist? Expect to produce their no-objection letters and an indemnity bond. Why it matters An unmutated register keeps showing the OLD owner though the sale is legally complete. Consequences compound: tax bills keep going to the previous owner while unpaid dues attach to the LAND, not the person; banks reject loans because mutation status is a basic ownership check; resale gets harder because the next buyer’s advocate flags the mismatch instantly; and heir disputes drag for years while land sits under a deceased owner’s name. Example: A buyer purchases in 2018, never mutates. In 2024 a tax-arrears notice arrives — the previous owner’s unpaid dues, now attached to the land. Then the bank declines a mortgage: “record shows a different owner”. Two problems, one skipped application that would have taken a few weeks in 2018. When to apply Immediately after any transaction — some states now run online or even automated mutation for straightforward transfers, others still take manual applications at the revenue office. The two classic delays: assuming the sale deed alone is enough, and inherited land sitting unmutated across a generation. Buying land that moved informally within a family? Ask whether mutation was completed at EACH step, not just the latest. Buying? Check mutation status first The seller-vs-record match is precisely the check that fails on an unmutated parcel — and it is checkable from outside (Dharani in Telangana shows the current pattadar). A mismatch does not always mean fraud; it always means an unfinished step someone must complete before your money moves. Quick answers (FAQ) Does mutation transfer ownership? No — registration does; mutation records it. How long does it take? Weeks for clean files; longer with objections. Can I sell unmutated land? Legally the registered owner can — practically, buyers and their banks balk; mutate first. Heir dispute during mutation? The revenue officer steps aside; civil court decides. Need a lawyer? Not for a clean application; yes the moment there is an objection. Mandatory for agricultural land? Effectively yes — the revenue record drives everything from tax to crop entries. Does it affect loans? Directly — lenders treat it as a gating check. Bottom line Easy to postpone, expensive to ignore. Mutation keeps your name accurate in the records that decide your tax bill, your loan eligibility and your next sale — apply promptly, and when buying, treat the seller’s mutation status as part of the title check. For you: Build it into your buyer experience: hand every plot purchaser a mutation-application pack at registration (or file it for them). Ventures whose buyers’ records are clean resell faster — and resales are your best advertising. On the acquisition side: an unmutated seller is a seller who cannot close on your timeline; surface it in week one, not at the SRO.
